title: Chapter 12 — Biographical
paragraphs: Queequeg was a native of Rokovoko, an island far away to the west and south. It isn't on any map; true places never are.

Even as a child running wild through the woods in nothing but a grass cloth, followed by nibbling goats as if he were a green sapling — even then, Queequeg's ambitious soul harbored a strong desire to see more of the Christian world than a whaling ship or two. His father was a High Chief, a King; his uncle a High Priest; and on his mother's side he boasted aunts married to unconquerable warriors. He had excellent blood in his veins — royal stuff, though sadly contaminated, I'm afraid, by the cannibal tendencies he'd picked up in his unschooled youth.

A ship from Sag Harbor visited his father's bay, and Queequeg tried to get passage to Christian lands. But the ship had a full crew and turned him down — even all the influence of his father the King couldn't help. So Queequeg made a vow. Alone in his canoe, he paddled to a distant strait that the ship had to pass through when leaving the island. On one side was a coral reef; on the other, a low tongue of land covered with mangrove thickets growing out into the water. Hiding his canoe among the thickets with its prow seaward, he sat in the stern, paddle in hand. When the ship glided past, he shot out like lightning, reached the ship's side, kicked his canoe over and sank it with one backward thrust of his foot, scrambled up the chains, and threw himself full-length on the deck, grabbing a ring-bolt. He swore not to let go even if they hacked him to pieces.

The captain threatened to throw him overboard and dangled a cutlass over his bare wrists. But Queequeg was a king's son, and Queequeg wouldn't budge. Struck by his desperate fearlessness and his wild desire to see Christendom, the captain finally relented and told him he could stay. But this fine young savage — this sea Prince of Wales — never saw the captain's cabin. They put him below with the sailors and made a whaleman of him. But like Czar Peter, content to toil in foreign shipyards, Queequeg didn't mind the indignity if it meant learning enough to help his people. At heart, he told me, he was driven by a deep desire to learn the arts of the Christians — to make his people happier and better than they already were. But alas, the practices of whalemen soon convinced him that even Christians could be miserable and wicked — infinitely more so than all his father's heathens. Arriving in Sag Harbor and seeing how the sailors lived there, then going on to Nantucket and seeing how they spent their wages — poor Queequeg gave up hope. It's a wicked world in every direction, he thought. I'll die a pagan.
And so, an idolator at heart, he lived among these Christians, wore their clothes, and tried to speak their language. That explained his odd ways, though he'd been away from home for some time.

Through hints, I asked whether he planned to go home and claim his throne — since his father, very old and feeble by last report, was probably dead by now. He said no, not yet. He was afraid that Christianity — or rather Christians — had made him unfit to ascend the pure, undefiled throne of thirty pagan kings before him. But eventually, he said, he would return — once he felt properly cleansed again. For now, he planned to sail around and sow his wild oats in all four oceans. They'd made him a harpooneer, and that barbed iron was his scepter now.

I asked about his immediate plans. He said he wanted to go to sea again in his old line of work. I told him whaling was my plan too, and that I intended to sail from Nantucket, the most promising port for an adventurous whaleman. He immediately decided to come with me — to ship on the same vessel, join the same watch, the same boat, the same mess — in short, to share every stroke of luck. With both my hands in his, we'd boldly dip into the potluck of both worlds. I agreed joyfully. Beyond the affection I now felt for Queequeg, he was an experienced harpooneer, which would be invaluable to someone like me — a complete novice at whaling, though well acquainted with the sea from merchant sailing.
His story finished with his pipe's last dying puff. Queequeg embraced me, pressed his forehead against mine, and blowing out the light, we rolled apart and were soon asleep.
